notes: These lines come from the prior year column of the filed T2 2024; the 2023 return itself is not in the folder.
CRA assessed it on 23 January 2024. The filing date is not recorded; a $904 fee to Saira on 18 January 2024 suggests she filed it.
The pro forma spreadsheet splits the same year differently (sub-contractors $25,000, office and sundry $7,828, net income before tax $40,095). The filed column is used here.
Revenue $72,923 less operating expenses $37,207 gives the $35,716 net income.

title: T2 2025
filed_by: Ejaz Pirwani, Fintax Associate Inc. (EFILE V3102)
plain: The corporation's 2025 return. Revenue $261,878, tax $13,368; instalments of $17,960 were already paid, so CRA refunded $4,592, which arrived with interest as $4,644.90 on 28 May 2026.
notes: Received and assessed by CRA on 18 May 2026. A resubmission on 19 May was rejected with error 387 because the year was already assessed. No formal notice of assessment is in the folder.
INDEX.md lists Claude's pre filing estimates under 'T2 filed and assessed' (net income $112,985.74, tax $14,146.58, retained earnings $156,216.16). Those are not the filed numbers.

The whole Mercedes lease was deducted at 100% business use without the s.67.3 cap: about $6,608 above the cap, about $9,600 if the down payment is also spread over the 36 month term (about $806 to $1,170 of tax). Left for Saira to decide.
Other expenses $5,332 is a balancing figure with no invoices behind it, per the accountant.
Taxes receivable $11,207 is corporate tax $4,898 plus GST $6,309. $4,898 is $306 more than the $4,592 refund, close to the $306.35 extra paid on the 2024 balance; not confirmed.

The instalment list on the return has two typing slips: 30 April shows year 2024, and the 30 December payment is listed as a second 30 October. Bank statements confirm the dates; the $17,960 total is right.
Salaries $17,838 is Maham's $16,000 plus the $1,837.50 payroll remittance.
The accountant's first draft (tax $15,989, refund $1,971) was replaced on 15 May by this version.

Also flagged on 7 October 2026: the Mercedes was claimed at 100% from 27 September to 31 December 2025 (a 20% personal share would be $3,771.76), and Umar's own car was paid mileage of $3,160.96 while about $3,270 of its actual costs were also deducted, a likely double claim.

title: T2 2026
plain: The corporation's 2026 return, year still running. On the 7 October projection tax would be about $15,243 against $10,500 of planned instalments, leaving about $4,743 to pay by 31 March 2027.

lines.label: Income added: 20% personal share of the Mercedes no longer deductible
Tax added by the Mercedes personal share
Lease payments above the s.67.3 cap (not deductible)
Director funded expenses needed to break even (23 September model)

notes: The 23 September projection counted only rent, phone, insurance and one service bill as director funded expenses ($11,133.96). The $45,273 break even includes those, so about $34,139 more would be needed; it predates the $578 Mercedes change.
An earlier estimate (taxable income $105,064, tax $12,818, about $2,318 short) dates from 3 August and wrongly subtracted the $4,644.90 refund from revenue.
Saira prepares it from a spreadsheet of every 2026 transaction, built after the December statements. Mercedes at 80%, rent at 30%.
The $4,644.90 CRA refund sits in the workbook's 2026 revenue columns and must be taken out.
Covering the gap by instalments means about $1,186 a month from September to December.
If Umar picks 85% business use instead of 80%, the personal charge becomes $5,339.61, deductions rise by $1,201.63 and the gap falls to about $4,596.

title: HST 2024-25
plain: HST for 15 August 2024 to 14 August 2025. Net tax was $35,121.50; the corporation paid $40,082 toward it and CRA refunded the $4,960.50 overpaid.
notes: Filed by NETFILE; never recalculate or refile.
CLAUDE.md says $28,400 was prepaid in 2025. That counts only March to September 2025 ($22,600 + $5,800) and leaves out $11,682 paid in December 2024.
A later ledger rebuilt the ITC total as $4,303.67; it wrongly counts the HST inside a CRA payment and is not comparable.
Sales are counted by the date received.

title: HST 2025-26
plain: HST for 15 August 2025 to 14 August 2026. The workpaper shows $23,595.34 of net tax against $26,000 already paid in instalments, so a refund of $2,404.66; Saira files it by 16 November 2026.

lines.label: HST paid on the lease in the year

notes: 14 November 2026 is a Saturday, so the due date is Monday 16 November.
The package sent on 23 September claimed the lease in full at 100% use: line 106 $5,372.45, refund $4,400.05. Revised on 7 October to 80% use plus the cap.
Saira says her books show more than ours; compare when her numbers arrive. She needs Represent a Client access to the RT account before filing.

Open questions for Saira: which list price sets the lease cap, 80% with no mileage log, three purchases without receipts, Valet receipts with no HST number, the Rogers credit (since answered: one credit, counted once, nothing owed), s.173 standby charge.
The instalments were paid on 20 October 2025 and 20 January, 20 April and 20 July 2026. The 15 September 2025 payment belongs to the year before.
The workpaper's Lease cap sheet gives the lease credit as $1,002.67 and the ITCs sheet as $1,002.69, a 2 cent rounding difference for Saira to settle.
If Umar picks 85% business use, the vehicle credits rise by about $112; that has to be settled before Saira files.

title: HST 2026-27
plain: The current HST year, 15 August 2026 to 14 August 2027. So far one MIR deposit of $8,542.80 is in it.
notes: Due three months after 14 August 2027; 14 November 2027 is a Sunday, so Monday 15 November.
The 21 August 2026 MIR deposit and the 31 August 2026 lease payment belong here, not in 2025-26.

Net tax runs above $3,000 a year, so quarterly instalments apply: about $5,898.84 each, due within one month after each quarter ends, so 14 December 2026, 15 March 2027 (14 March is a Sunday), 14 June 2027 and 14 September 2027. Worked out from the CRA rule; check with Saira.
